newsitem.title: ITALY: motor racing - Ferrari anniversary brings Formula 1 to Rome streets.
newsitem.headline: motor racing - Ferrari anniversary brings Formula 1 to Rome streets.

text.p: The dreams of every car-crazed Roman came true on Sunday when Ferrari marked its 50th anniversary by bringing the sights and sounds of motor racing to the ancient streets of the Italian capital.

Some 270 of the world's most exclusive and expensive Ferraris, driven by their owners and Formula One greats, roared and reverberated through steady rain along the banks of the Tiber river, over cobblestones and past ruins.

Germany's former world champion Michael Schumacher and Briton Eddie Irvine were in action, skidding their howling red F1 cars round a slippery rainsoaked circuit as if they were racing for real and coming in for swift pitstops.

The two team mates drove together in the afternoon around an empty street circuit usually clogged with traffic in a city where many a driver pretends his battered Fiat has Ferrari's prancing horse motif on its bonnet.

Italian Franco Cortese had given the firm's late founder Enzo Ferrari his first victory in the Rome Grand Prix of May 25, 1947 on the circuit round the Circus Maximus and the Baths of Caracalla, with the Colosseum as a backdrop.

On Sunday, the old memories came flooding back in an outpouring of affection as Ferrari celebrated that first triumph with a run around the original track after parading past the city's best known monuments in the morning.

"How beautiful were those races of long ago, amongst the houses, through the city streets filled with the smell of petrol and oil of cars and the straw of safety bales," reminisced Giovanni Agnelli, whose Fiat car firm now owns Ferrari.

"If I had to define in a few adjectives what makes a Ferrari, I would say it is fascinating, victorious and as precious as any jewel," Agnelli wrote in an article in the daily Gazzetta dello Sport newspaper.
A less well-heeled Italian spectator, asked what he would do to own a Ferrari, replied: "Anything".

Since the early days, Ferrari has won nine Formula One drivers' world titles, eight F1 constructors' world titles and 109 Formula One victories, the latest this year with Schumacher driving at Monte Carlo.
It is the only manufacturer to have competed in every Formula One world championship since the outset in 1950 and the only one to build every part of its cars in-house.
Jose Froilan Gonzalez of Argentina, the corpulent "Pampas Bull" who was Ferrari's first driver to win a Formula One race at Silverstone in 1951, was back for the occasion.

His 375 car and Schumacher's current F1 car had been parked earlier in the week on either side of the Roman equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in the Capitol square designed by Michelangelo, attracting crowds of curious tourists.

South African Jody Scheckter -- the most recent driver to win the world championship for Ferrari in 1979 -- and former champions Phil Hill of the United States and John Surtees of Britain also rolled back the years.

"When you drive for Ferrari its a really special relationship," Scheckter told Reuters. "I drove one of the cars similar to mine about five years ago. Since then I haven't driven anything. It brings back memories."
One notable absentee was Ferrari's former world champion Niki Lauda, recovering from a kidney transplant.
The Austrian's car was driven by Italian Arturo Merzario, a former Ferrari driver who helped pull him from his flaming car after a near-fatal Grand Prix crash in 1976.
"For me driving for Ferrari was the best," Lauda told Italian television by telephone from Austria.
"Working with Enzo Ferrari was fantastic. He was a man with a big heart, who only wanted to win races."
The racers were accompanied by scores of wealthy private owners whose cars were flown in for the occasion from as far afield as Japan, South Africa and the United States.

The Ferraris included an ivory-coloured 375MM bought by Italian film director Roberto Rossellini for his wife Ingrid Bergman in the 1950s and a black 250 GT 2+2 used by Rome police in the 1960s for high-speed chases.
They were parked overnight at the Stadio dei Marmi, next to the Olympic stadium, with guards posted to watch over what amounted to the world's most expensive car park.
The cars leave Rome on Monday along the route of the old Mille Miglia race with stops in Siena and Florence before arriving at Fiorano near Ferrari's birthplace of Modena.

"Maybe Enzo Ferrari would say that we're making a bit too much of a show of it," said Ferrari president Luca Di Montezemolo of the party. "But I think that, deep down, he would be almost as happy as we all are."
